scenes.narration: From Jenkins to GitHub Actions. Chapter two: analyse, convert, and validate.
onScreen: Moving one Jenkins pipeline to GitHub Actions, step by step

scenes.source: README Parts 2 to 4; source-facts.md do-not-claim list
scenes.narration: A quick note on what this chapter is. We take one example pipeline and run three automatic steps on it. The output is replayed from real runs. This chapter does not show that the new workflow behaves the same as the old one. That is tested later. It also has not been run on GitHub.
onScreen: Three local, automatic steps on one example pipeline
Output is replayed from real runs
Not shown here: proof the new workflow behaves the same
Not shown here: any run on GitHub

data.foot: Checking the structure is not the same as proving the behaviour.

scenes.narration: The starting point is a Jenkins pipeline: a file telling Jenkins how to build, test and deploy a small service. GitHub Actions can do the same job, with different vocabulary and rules. The harness tackles the move in three steps. Read and score. Write the new version. Check it for mistakes.

onScreen.v: Analyse: read the pipeline and score the difficulty
Convert: write the GitHub Actions workflow and a report
Validate: check structure, security and policy

beats.narration: Step one, analyse. The tool reads the pipeline using the same Groovy engine that Jenkins itself uses, so it understands the file the way Jenkins does. Then it gives a difficulty score.

highlight.text: Difficulty twenty-three: assisted, meaning a person helps

beats.narration: The analysis also writes a results page. Its findings list the parts that will need attention. There is an approval gate on the deploy stage. There are conditions written in Groovy. There is a schedule using a Jenkins shorthand that GitHub does not have. And there are two stored credentials.

Step two, convert. It produces nine jobs and sorts every construct into a bucket. Forty-one mapped cleanly. Thirty-three were approximated, which means a close equivalent, not an identical one. One needs a person. Overall, eighty-one percent was automated.

scenes.source: README Part 3 job table; capture supporting #1
scenes.narration: Why nine jobs? In Jenkins, the stages share one workspace. GitHub Actions jobs do not, so the converter splits the work up, and hands the files on from one job to the next. The first two stages become one job. The three parallel quality checks become three jobs. Then come the compatibility matrix and publish. Before deploy, a small gate job decides whether deploy should run at all, so a skipped deploy never asks for approval. A final job reports the overall result.

data.title: Nine jobs in the converted workflow

beats.narration: Here are the job names, read straight from the generated workflow file.

Conditions are translated too. A Jenkins rule that says, skip this stage for snapshot versions, becomes an if line in the GitHub expression language. A schedule using the Jenkins shorthand becomes a fixed time. The deploy job also names a protected environment, which is where a person will have to add the reviewers.

highlight.text: A Jenkins when rule becomes an if condition
Reviewers must be added by a person

beats.narration: The migration report lists every construct with its line number and status. Three things are dropped because GitHub has no equivalent: an unstable post condition, the build discarder and timestamps. One is manual, an assignment that renames the build. Its header calls the automated share an effort estimate, not a measure of correctness. Reading this report is where a human adds value.

highlight.text: Approximated items also deserve a review
81 percent is an effort estimate, not correctness

beats.narration: Step three, validate. Three checkers look at the new workflow. The first checks its structure, including the shell scripts inside it. The second looks for security problems. The third applies the project's own rules. Both standard tools found nothing. The rules raised one warning, and the overall result is okay.

highlight.text: policy 1: a warning, not a failure

beats.narration: That warning points at a line in the final job. It still contains a placeholder, because the converter could not translate a Jenkins value that holds the build result. The placeholder is marked with a TODO. That is the tool telling you where a human is needed.

highlight.text: Untranslated Groovy value left as a TODO

scenes.title: What we did, and what is left
scenes.narration: To sum up. Analysis scored the pipeline as assisted, with findings to review. Conversion automated about eighty-one percent and listed the rest in a report. Validation found no structural or security problems, and one warning. A person must still review the approximated and manual items, fix the warning, and add reviewers to the deploy environment. And passing these checks does not prove the workflow behaves like the original. The next chapter tests that.
onScreen: Convert: 9 jobs, 81.0 percent automated, plus a report

onScreen.text: Still needed: human review, fix the warning, add deploy reviewers
Not proven: that the workflow behaves like the Jenkinsfile
